meta.description: Orwell never wrote it. The wording is a 1993 paraphrase by critic Richard Grenier, later quote-marked and pinned on Orwell — and on Churchill.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People sleep peaceably in their beds at night only because rough men stand ready to do violence on their behalf'?
meta.ogDescription: Orwell never wrote it. The wording is a 1993 paraphrase by critic Richard Grenier, later quote-marked and misattributed to Orwell and Churchill.

answer.label: Not Orwell’s words — a 1993 paraphrase by Richard Grenier
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Orwellian — he wrote that civilization depends on “other men… there to guard and feed” it — but this exact sentence is not his. The wording was written by critic Richard Grenier in an April 1993 column, as his own summary of Orwell’s view, with no quotation marks ↗. Only later did others put it in quotes and hang it on Orwell.

source.excerpt: As George Orwell pointed out, people sleep peacefully in their beds at night only because rough men stand ready to do violence on their behalf.
trail: The definitive investigation is Quote Investigator, which found the phrasing in Richard Grenier’s 6 April 1993 Washington Times column ↗ — presented without quotation marks as a paraphrase of Orwell.

What Orwell did write is in his essay on Kipling: “men can only be highly civilized while other men, inevitably less civilized, are there to guard and feed them ↗” — a related thought, but not this sentence.
By 1998, columnist George F. Will had amplified a variant (“rough men stand ready in the night to visit violence”) ↗, and the line hardened into a fake Orwell — and later Churchill — quotation.
source.excerptNote: Grenier’s original 1993 sentence — note there were no quotation marks around it. He was paraphrasing Orwell, not quoting him. Later writers added the quote marks and the phrasing drifted (“peaceably,” “sleep safely,” “visit violence”).

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is not from a public-domain Orwell text at all — it originated in Richard Grenier’s 1993 Washington Times column, so the sentence as phrased is a modern (1993) work and in copyright. Orwell’s genuine, related passages appear in works first published in the 1940s, themselves still in copyright in the US.

author.heading: About George Orwell
author.bio: George Orwell (pen name of Eric Arthur Blair) was an English writer whose Animal Farm (1945) and Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) made him one of the 20th century’s most-quoted authors on power and politics. In his 1942 essay on Kipling he did argue that the civilized depend on rougher men to guard them — but he never wrote the polished “rough men stand ready” sentence. Being a magnet for pointed political one-liners, he is among the most misquoted writers online.

misattribution.heading: How Orwell got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “paraphrase-hardened-into-a-quote” case: a critic’s honest summary of Orwell’s view was later dressed in quotation marks and sold as Orwell’s own words.

items.why: Orwell never wrote this sentence in any book, essay, letter, or broadcast. Quote Investigator found no instance in his works ↗; the closest real passages are looser and differently worded.
The line is frequently pinned on Churchill too, but Hillsdale’s Churchill Project finds no evidence he ever said it ↗.

items.scope: The real author of the wording
items.why: Grenier wrote “As George Orwell pointed out, people sleep peacefully in their beds at night only because rough men stand ready to do violence on their behalf” — as a paraphrase, with no quotation marks ↗. Others added the marks.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Orwell’s (by way of Kipling); the memorable wording is Richard Grenier’s 1993 paraphrase, later misquoted as a direct Orwell — and Churchill — line, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: The genuine Orwell behind the fake quote
lead: Orwell’s real argument, in his 1942 essay on Rudyard Kipling, was that comfortable civilians are hypocrites about the force that protects them. He praised Kipling’s line about “making mock of uniforms that guard you while you sleep” as a perfect skewering of “the one-eyed pacifism of the English,” and wrote that “men can only be highly civilized while other men, inevitably less civilized, are there to guard and feed them.”

In “Notes on Nationalism” (1945) he made the point again: those who “abjure” violence “can only do so because others are committing violence on their behalf.” The sentiment is unmistakably Orwell’s — which is exactly why Grenier’s tidy 1993 restatement was so easy to mistake for a real quotation.
context.pull: The idea is Orwell’s. The sentence is Grenier’s.
